theme: The thick envelope of fall mail: ask a parent what they make of it, not whether they did it right, and let a normal call be about the tomatoes.

posts.text: A thick envelope lands in your parents' mailbox every fall. The easy question is "did you open it?" The better one is "what did you make of it?" They have been reading their own mail for a long time.
posts.alt: Three-panel comic. June sits at her kitchen table with a thick envelope, a mug and a phone. Sam, far away, asks on the phone, 'Did the letter come?' June answers, 'It did. Pen's in my hand.' Caption: She had it handled.

posts.title: How to ask a parent about their mail without taking over
posts.text:
How to ask a parent about their mail without taking over

Three small steps for a call about a letter: ask what they think of it, let them explain it, then offer a second pair of eyes and wait for the yes.
posts.alt: Three stacked comic panels. Sam walks outside among autumn leaves asking, 'What did you make of the letter?' June explains at her table, 'Same plan, but the price moved.' Sam offers, 'Want a second pair of eyes?' Captions: Ask what they think of it. Let them explain it. Offer help, then wait for the yes.

posts.title: Let the normal morning be enough

script.say: Every fall, a thick envelope shows up in your parents' mailbox. And the next call turns into a quiz.
script.overlay: The call turns into a quiz
script.broll: Founder to camera, kitchen counter behind him.

script.say: Did you open it? Did you read it? Did you take your pills? I'd rather just ask how they are.
script.overlay: I'd rather ask how they are

script.say: So I built Kettle. It notices that a normal morning happened on the phone they already own, and tells us twice a day. If a morning is different, it asks them first.
script.overlay: Twice a day. Asks them first.
script.broll: Neutral b-roll: a plain phone face down on a kitchen table, no app visible.

script.say: Then the call can be about tomatoes.
script.overlay: Then the call can be about tomatoes

posts.text: The call turns into a quiz. It does not have to.

posts.text: Some calls turn into a list. The letter, the gutters, the appointment. Then a parent says she is out with the tomatoes, and that is the call you wanted.
posts.alt: Three-panel comic. Sam frowns at his desk, writing a list and saying, 'Okay, and how is the letter, the pills, the gutters...' June, in the garden with gloves and a watering can, says, 'I'm out with the tomatoes.' Sam laughs and says, 'Tell me about the tomatoes.' Captions: The call turned into a list. Better call.

posts.title: Questions to ask a parent that are not a quiz
posts.text:
Questions to ask a parent that are not a quiz

Start with what is on their table. Ask about the day, not the paperwork. Let the letter wait for the end of the call.
posts.alt: Three stacked comic panels. June reads a library book in an armchair. Sam on a train asks, 'What are you reading?' Sam and June on a video call, her pen and envelope to one side. Captions: Start with what is on their table. Ask about the day, not the paperwork. The letter can wait for the end.

posts.title: Her own mail

script.say: My parents have been reading their own mail for decades.
When I call about a letter, I try to ask what they think of it, not whether they did it right.
script.overlay: What do you think of it?
script.broll: Phone on a table, a pen and an envelope beside it.

script.say: They know their own business. My job is to be on the phone, and to ask if they want a second pair of eyes.
script.overlay: Offer a second pair of eyes

script.say: Then I wait for the yes.

posts.text: Ask what they think. Then wait for the yes.
posts.alt: Cover: June sits at her kitchen table with a mug, an envelope and a pen, reading her own mail, the green kettle behind her. Caption: She was reading her own mail.
